title: The Narrows
text:
On the eighteenth day <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> went to see the parts man on <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-b3f9-763c-9191-79ee3280bae1">Ashland</entity> about a throttle cable. The cable on the bike had stretched twelve millimeters at the barrel end. He'd been nursing it for three weeks and was done nursing it.

He'd bought from Cho on <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-b3f9-763c-9191-79ee3280bae1">Ashland</entity> for six years. The man sourced <entity repo="corponation" guid="80a78887-98cf-4aa2-96fc-97c62a84fd21">Axiom</entity>-era hardware out of a storefront the size of a wide closet, sold nothing he couldn't hold up to the light, and had never once been out of anything <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> needed. The stretch was survivable on surface streets, but it put a half-second of slack between what he asked the bike to do and what it did. In a corridor, that half-second could get him killed.

"Throttle cable," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

Cho was already moving. He opened the first drawer, held it to the light, closed it. Opened a second. His hands slowed. He opened a third, stood with his back to <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> for a moment that went three seconds too long, and turned around wearing the face of a man who'd rehearsed an apology until it came out flat.

"Throttle cable," Cho said. "I had some."

"You always have some."

"I'm currently out." He gestured at nothing. "I can check with the <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-c53d-7304-b953-a44879ea410e">Damen</entity> yard."

Behind his shoulder, the third drawer was still open an inch. The label was in Cho's own hand — the cable spec, <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s spec, written there because <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had needed it often enough that Cho had labeled the drawer to save time. The drawer was not empty. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> could see the shape of coiled cable through the gap.

"Thanks," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said, and walked out. There was nothing in the conversation worth finishing.

He rode home with the slack still in the cable. The half-second was still there.

The carrier who ran his packages was a woman named <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a5f9-7bce-bc4e-8af3094f3073">Freya</entity>. She worked out of the <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-95c2-7084-bc60-1d8cb35562ed">Bucktown</entity> freight level and hadn't been late once in four years. The next morning, at 07:00, she stopped answering. Not a queue. Not a delay. Her terminal took his reads and never delivered them, the way a door takes a knock and never opens.

He had a job going that week — a skip-trace in the <entity repo="place" guid="019ece26-b83d-7708-9ade-347fcbf63b44">Pilsen corridor</entity>, a client sitting on it, Φ40 on the back end if the documentation landed before a civil filing deadline. He spent two hours routing around <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a5f9-7bce-bc4e-8af3094f3073">Freya</entity>, through her backup and through the Loop carrier that <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-608f-7b15-887d-1fe5473de7d5">Ria</entity> used. <entity repo="place" guid="01a01887-b5f4-781c-8d38-122f7e1f38ba">The Loop</entity> carrier told him, politely, that she was running at capacity. He sent the documentation by a walk-courier service on Halsted for a Φ12 surcharge, and it arrived twenty minutes past the filing window. The client paid the base fee and declined the back end. That was their right.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> sat at the far end of his table, a casing half-open, her tools fanned out. She asked, without looking up, if he'd tried the backup.

"Lost twelve on the courier," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "Forty on the filing. Fifty-two total."

She set down her loupe.

"How many doors?" she asked.

"<entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-b3f9-763c-9191-79ee3280bae1">Ashland</entity> is one. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a5f9-7bce-bc4e-8af3094f3073">Freya</entity> is two. I found four more this morning — fixers who aren't returning calls. A rigger named Goss who normally takes anything with a fee."

"Goss." The word had a flat edge. She'd used Goss twice and found him solid. "That's deliberate?"

"Yes."

The kettle went. She filled both cups and set his down, handle first, and went back to the casing. Neither of them said the thing they both understood: it had started, they were inside it, and the only question left was how far it would go.

He went through the rest of the list that afternoon, in order, the way he checked anything he needed to trust. Six more names. Six people who owed him nothing but had answered when he called, because they understood that a favor banked was a favor that might one day pull code out of your hardware before it killed you.

Three didn't answer at all — not busy, not away, just gone, their terminals returning the polite silence of a line that had been quietly retired. Rue was one of them. Rue who'd calibrated his neuretics three times, who'd never once asked what the fragments in his hardware were or whose they'd been. The call went through. He heard the drill running somewhere in her workspace, heard her breathing on the other end — and then the line went dead. Not a voice. Not an apology. The sound of her choosing not to answer.

Two answered and found reasons. A schedule conflict that hadn't existed yesterday. A supplier problem that wouldn't specify which supplier. Both spoke in the flat, careful tone of someone reading from a script they'd written in advance, the words laid down before he'd finished saying their names.

The sixth picked up on the first ring — which was already wrong, because she never picked up on the first ring — recognized his voice, and hung up without a word. That told him more than any of the others had. <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> chosen on purpose reads different from silence that just happens.

He sat with the six names crossed out and did the arithmetic he didn't want to do. Cho. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a5f9-7bce-bc4e-8af3094f3073">Freya</entity>. Goss. Six more this afternoon. Nine doors, and every one of them closed by somebody who'd never once had to explain themselves to <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>, because they didn't answer to him. They answered to whoever was calling in favors faster than he could spend them.

The terminal's screen had gone dark between calls, and it gave him back his own face — the scar tissue at his temple where the neuretics had integrated, the flat expression he'd worn so long it had stopped being a choice. A man watching his own infrastructure collapse into a pattern.

Whoever it was hadn't come for him directly. Not yet. They were taking the ground out from under him first, one contact at a time, the way you starve a fire by pulling the wood before you ever have to fight the flame.

The kettle had gone cold on the stove. He didn't move to heat it again.

On the nineteenth morning the crew's logbook had a new entry.

08:44 — KID ON THE STOOP. DRY COAT. CAR MONEY. ASKED FOR BOSS. HANDED OVER AN ENVELOPE AND LEFT. DID NOT TAKE A DUMPLING (OFFERED). SUSPICIOUS.
NOTE FROM RAFTERS: DREW HIS FACE. FOR THE FILE. VERY UNMEMORABLE FACE. THIS IS SUSPICIOUS.

The envelope was heavy card stock, the kind that costs more than whatever is written inside. Within it was a cream rectangle: one hand-brushed line above a stamped blossom — five petals, open, no name. The script was precise and unhurried, the kind of penmanship a person learns when it still means something, when it can't be templated or forged by a machine that doesn't tire.

BRING THE SWORD.

Below the blossom, an address in the Narrows and a time. 20:00.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> set it on the table beside Sable's card. The two of them made a small pile he didn't like the look of. He turned the summons over in the light the way Cho held hardware — no watermark, no maker's mark, no secondary text. Someone had decided the blossom was enough, and the Narrows address was enough, and the fact that they knew about the sword was enough. He went to find the sword instead — the summons could wait until he'd confirmed the thing was even still his to bring.

The locker under the floorboards was empty. Not forced, not disturbed — empty, the felt lining pressed flat where <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity> had lain, as if nothing had ever weighed on it. He knelt there longer than he needed to, running his thumb along the seam, and the crew's chatter in the front room went on without him, ignorant. He'd checked this locker two mornings ago, the way you're certain of a thing you touch every time you pass it — the weight of it, the presence, the never having to wonder. Someone with a very unmemorable face had known exactly where to look, and had come and gone before the eighteenth morning ever started. The card on the table wasn't an invitation. It was a receipt. Whoever wrote BRING THE SWORD already had it, and wanted to see if <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> would show up empty-handed and lie, or show up empty-handed and beg — and he had no way to tell which answer got the crew killed.

He closed the locker and set the board back over it anyway. The gesture meant something, even if it changed nothing.

He went to find clean clothes.

<entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a948-7b0e-9b15-63f753f313c9">The Narrows</entity> announced itself by what it didn't have.

Every streetlight worked. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> counted the first three, then stopped, because the rhythm never broke. In West Town you learned the dead lights by season — the black stretch on Milwaukee, the dark third post the block had quietly routed its foot traffic around since last autumn. Here the lights ran even and unbroken, every one of them, and the steadiness of it put something cold up his spine. Not a threat. The feeling of a place that had been kept, carefully, for a long time, by someone who didn't need to say so.

He was here for one thing: to reach the arcade address, find the woman <entity repo="faction" guid="019d6143-a893-7801-860b-0eda6a216393">Lotus</entity> called the Narrows' bookkeeper, and walk out with her name on his side of the ledger before the night shift changed. Do that, and West Town ate for a month. Miss it, and he'd made the trip for nothing.

The gutters were clear. No tags on the support pillars. The corners were staffed by people who stood the way staff stand, not sentinels — they watched without making a show of watching, took up space without guarding it, marked him on the way in and let their eyes drift back to the middle distance. Nobody begged. Nobody moved at odd angles.

He found the address two blocks in: a covered arcade between two buildings, open at both ends, roofed in mesh strung with grow-strips close enough to touch. In steel collars bolted to the uprights, eleven cherry trees grew.

He stopped.

They were in bloom — white going to a pink with blood in it, not the tired pink of forced spring stock but a deliberate color, the kind it takes years of breeding to hold in the wrong month. Lights buried in the collars threw the <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aab1-78aa-8d59-ad014f931b0f">glow up</entity> through the roots, catching each blossom from below. Loose petals lay on the wet concrete in small, exact clusters. He stood with petals settling on his coat. The trees were engineered and expensive, paid for with every tariff <entity repo="faction" guid="019d6143-a893-7801-860b-0eda6a216393">Lotus</entity> had charged the Narrows since someone planted the first collar. They were also beautiful. Both were true.

Six children ran circuits under the arcade, screaming on the inhale at the pitch of a body moving faster than it can hold. Nobody hushed them.

Then the staff at the far end folded in, and the way through the arcade stopped being a way.

They didn't rush him. That was the trouble. Four of them peeled off their corners and drifted into the open mouth of the arcade the same unhurried way they'd watched him come in — not a wall, just a narrowing, bodies filling the space where the path had been. One of the children scooped up mid-run and set on a hip, out of the lane, casual as clearing a table. The screaming didn't stop. That was worse, somehow: nothing here treated this as an event.

The one in front had her hands in her coat pockets and no weapon showing, which told him more than a weapon would have. She was positioned there — not waiting for anyone, not browsing, just standing in the exact center of the lane with the specific stillness of someone who knew to the inch how much space her body took up. She had the kind of face he wouldn't have been able to describe an hour later, and he understood that was a skill and not an accident.

"You're early," she said. Her voice was neutral, not hostile. That was worse. "Bookkeeper doesn't take walk-ins, and she doesn't take West Town at all. Somebody sold you a name that isn't for sale." She tilted her head at the trees, at him standing in the fallen petals. "Shift changes at twenty-one hundred. You can go back the way you came while the light's still good. Or you can wait for the shift to change and explain yourself to the people who don't ask twice."

Behind him, unhurried, two more corners came off their posts.

Go back and he'd made the trip for nothing — West Town went hungry, and <entity repo="faction" guid="019d6143-a893-7801-860b-0eda6a216393">Lotus</entity> had sent him into a door that was never open? Push forward and there was no forward; the arcade had closed like a fist that had known his shape before he'd stepped inside. The shift changed in minutes either way, and both of the choices she'd offered him were the same choice, walked out to sound like two: leave with nothing.

Petals kept coming down. Nobody hushed the children.

The ramen-ya was eight stools and a cedar counter and a door that stood open.

He counted the stools on the way in. The cedar was hand-planed and gone gold from years of handling, worn smooth by elbows and the weight of people who came here because they knew what they'd get. Behind it the cook worked with the tight economy of a man who'd shed every wasted motion long ago. Four of the other stools were taken: a man in his forties with a collapsed baton at his hip, a woman with a vibro-edge unit in a shoulder rig, a younger man <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> read as wired by the way he held his neck, and an empty jacket at the far end that had left a cup and a short blade on the counter beside it.

Weapons worn openly. Nothing checked at the door but behavior.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> hung his coat on the hook at the entrance — the only hook, set there by someone who understood guests — and sat on the last open stool. The cook looked at him once, turned to the pot, and started building a bowl. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> hadn't ordered. The cook didn't ask.

The bowl came in three stages. The broth first: the color of good age, smelling of something started days ago and tended since. Then the noodles, hand-pulled, dropped in with just enough time left to finish cooking in the broth. Then the fat, rendered thin and even, a bright lens across the surface. From somewhere under the counter the cook set down a half-round of soft-boiled egg, split with the knife held sideways so the yolk stayed whole.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> ate the first mouthful.

He understood at once what the bowl was for. Not hospitality, exactly — an argument, made in fat and salt and twenty years of practice. The argument was: we make things correctly here. That was probably the whole point of it.

He was most of the way through when the door changed.

The open frame filled without the light changing — someone standing in it who knew <entity repo="document" guid="5de87125-d108-6ae9-edf1-9866e655c9b5">how to stand</entity> so the light didn't. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> didn't turn. He watched the cook instead, and the cook's hands, which had not stopped once since he sat down, stopped now. The bright economy went out of them. The knife lay still on the cedar. That told <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> everything the door didn't.

Then the empty jacket at the far end wasn't empty; the owner had come back from wherever he'd been and was already reaching for the short blade, and the man with the collapsed baton was on his feet with the wall at his back, and the wired kid had turned his whole body toward <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> — not toward the door.

Toward <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>.

He'd read the room wrong. He'd counted the stools and the weapons and the exits and he'd missed the only thing that mattered, which was that every person in here had known he was coming, and had ordered him a bowl, and had let him finish most of it first. They had arranged themselves in the space like furniture, so neither one had a wall at his back, so the sight lines to the door and the kitchen belonged to them. The cook set the knife down flat on the cedar, well out of <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s reach, and stepped back from the counter, and did not meet his eyes.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s coat was on the hook by the door. The door was the only way out. And the door was where the standing man was.

The <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6ea-84c8-7ad6-89f8-32630940e563">Branch</entity> Manager came through the doorway like a man who had walked this route for years and didn't need to announce it. Umbrella furled and tucked under his arm. Mid-sixties. A suit with no concession to fashion — not old-fashioned, not plain, just chosen once by a man who understood fabric and had never needed to think about it again. He was half a head shorter than <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>, and he had the stillness of someone who had never needed to take up space to fill a room.

Everyone at the counter got an inch and a half taller when he came in.

Not in any way you could put a number to. The body knew it before the mind caught up: the man who ran this territory had arrived, and the room was better for it. He hung the umbrella on the hook next to <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s jacket — the only hook, which meant he'd known it was there — sat at the empty jacket's stool, claimed his cup, and drank from it like a man picking up a sentence he'd stepped away from.

He looked at <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s face.

"You took the clerk out," the <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6ea-84c8-7ad6-89f8-32630940e563">Branch</entity> Manager said. "Fourteen people in that corridor. Our people. Several of them went home the worse for it."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> waited. His ribs ached when he shifted.

"The contract was legitimate," the <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6ea-84c8-7ad6-89f8-32630940e563">Branch</entity> Manager said. "Your conduct was correct. Our crew engaged first." He turned his cup once in both hands. "We pay for what we break. It's most of what we are. The hold lifted this evening — the seven doors, the carrier on the Spine, the parts man on <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-b3f9-763c-9191-79ee3280bae1">Ashland</entity>." He paused. "Cho is easily embarrassed about these things. He has the cable for you. With apologies, priced at list. The apologies are real. The pricing is how we mean them."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> ate the last mouthful of the bowl.

"I appreciate it," he said.

"The fifty-two," the <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6ea-84c8-7ad6-89f8-32630940e563">Branch</entity> Manager said, flat.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> looked at him.

"The filing gap. The courier surcharge. Cho's hold cost you more than he cost you in stock." The <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6ea-84c8-7ad6-89f8-32630940e563">Branch</entity> Manager set his cup down. "The apology covers the doors. The doors cover everything behind them. Priced at list."

He reached into his coat and set a small envelope on the cedar. Not in <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s space. Close enough to mean it.

"Good?" the <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6ea-84c8-7ad6-89f8-32630940e563">Branch</entity> Manager asked, and looked at the bowl.

"Best in the city."

"That," said the <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6ea-84c8-7ad6-89f8-32630940e563">Branch</entity> Manager, with the small satisfaction of a man whose point has landed, "is probably why it's the bowl." He put two fingers on the counter's edge, thinking. "I have a second piece of business. Not a condition. The freeze lifts either way."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> waited.

"I'm offering you a spot on payroll. House colors. Infrastructure — parts, carrying, the counters in every territory we hold, a legal team that files for you and bills us. You stop taking work from people who don't understand what they're asking for. In five years, if the work is what I think it is, a chair at this counter with your name in the wood." He touched the cedar's edge. "The cedar decides, in the end. It keeps certain names."

"No," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "I don't wear colors."

The <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6ea-84c8-7ad6-89f8-32630940e563">Branch</entity> Manager did not look surprised. He looked like a man reaching a conclusion he'd come in expecting.

"The clerk who sat in that seat nine years ago said exactly that," he said. "In exactly that tone. She'd been doing piece work in the Narrows for three years. She said no, I don't wear colors, and then she sat down anyway. It took eleven months and one specific kind of trouble she didn't want to carry alone. She runs the <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-95c2-7084-bc60-1d8cb35562ed">Bucktown</entity> counting room now." He picked up his cup. "The offer stands. Standing offers are how we say please."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> looked at the counter. <entity repo="material" guid="d6cc00f6-2360-9a5d-5f6c-3a1996617b06">Cedar</entity> gone gold with years of handling. He could see where the grain ran different under the finish — the darker sections at the older stools, the pale ones at the new. His stool was neither. Somewhere in the middle.

He understood the offer for what it was. He would come back for the bowl. When he came back, the offer would still be standing, because that was the whole design. The courtesy was the hook, and the hook was the point. The fifty-two would feed West Town for a month. The colors would have fed it forever, and made every contract after this a negotiation with people who already owned him.

"I'll remember it," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

"That's all it asks," said the <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6ea-84c8-7ad6-89f8-32630940e563">Branch</entity> Manager. He rose, took his cup to the far end of the counter, and the whole room gained its inch and a half again.

The lacquered case came up from behind the counter before anyone had said the word sword. The cook set it in front of <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>, stepped back, and found something to do at the far burner. Inside, on gray felt that matched the locker's, <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> lay exactly as it had left West Town — saya unmarked, edge untouched, nothing about it to say it had crossed the city in someone else's hands.

"Returned," the <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6ea-84c8-7ad6-89f8-32630940e563">Branch</entity> Manager said, as if the word settled a small invoice. "The borrowing was a question. You answered it by coming."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> took the sword and did not ask what the question had been. The anger he folded flat and put away; it would be useful somewhere else.

The togishi was at the far end of the counter, between the wire's stool and the wall, working the cook's knives.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> hadn't noticed him arrive. Maybe he'd always been there — one of those people who fill a space so completely they're part of the scene before you count them. Small. Ten years older than the <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6ea-84c8-7ad6-89f8-32630940e563">Branch</entity> Manager. He had the hands of a man whose whole trade was patience. He ran the whetstone down a blade slowly, the way you read something rather than fix it, each pass a question and an answer.

The cook's knives were good blades. The togishi handled them like things meant to outlast him.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> watched a while, because watching was the only polite thing to do.

"Φ1," he said, eventually.

The togishi looked up. He looked at <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity>'s saya.

"Φ1 for what?" he asked.

"Your read on <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity>. One minute."

"<entity repo="character" guid="019eb6ea-e248-74dd-b603-8b19f4c3ad6a">Togishi</entity> does not work by the minute," the togishi said, and held out his hand.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> paid first, because that was how it was done, and laid <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> across the man's open palms.

The togishi held it without drawing, hands flat, feeling the balance travel through his grip. Then he drew it, slow, and turned it to the light from outside — the cherry-tree light, pink-white through the arcade opening, falling soft on the face of <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity>.
